groups.name: Inner Planets
groups.summary: These are the four rocky planets inside the asteroid belt.
groups.description: These are the four rocky planets inside the asteroid belt. They are smaller than the gas giants, and they have solid surfaces you could actually stand on. Pick one planet to see its numbers.

objects.name: Mercury
objects.summary: Almost no atmosphere, so day and night temperatures are extreme.
objects.description: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It does not have a real atmosphere to hold heat, so the ground goes from extremely hot in the day to extremely cold at night.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: About 167°C on average, with a huge day-night swing

objects.name: Venus
objects.summary: About Earth's size, but the surface is much hotter.
objects.description: Venus is close to Earth in size, but the surface is nothing like ours. A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, which is why Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

objects.name: Earth
objects.summary: The only planet here with oceans and known life.
objects.description: Earth is the planet we live on. Liquid water stays on the surface, and it is the only place we know that has life. The distance from the Sun is a big part of why the average temperature is mild.

objects.name: Mars
objects.summary: Smaller and colder than Earth, with a thin atmosphere.
objects.description: Mars is the red planet. It is colder and smaller than Earth, and its atmosphere is thin. It still gets a lot of attention because it has polar ice and signs of old water.

groups.name: Outer Planets
groups.summary: These four sit past the asteroid belt.
groups.description: These four sit past the asteroid belt. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. You do not get a solid surface the way you do with the inner planets. Pick a planet to see its size, distance, orbit, and temperature.

objects.name: Jupiter
objects.summary: The largest planet, made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
objects.description: Jupiter is the largest planet. Most of it is hydrogen and helium, not rock. The Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has lasted for hundreds of years.

objects.name: Saturn
objects.summary: A gas giant known for its bright ice rings.
objects.description: Saturn is the planet with the obvious rings. Those rings are mostly chunks of ice. The planet itself is a gas giant, and it is light for its size.

objects.name: Uranus
objects.summary: An ice giant that rotates on its side.
objects.description: Uranus is an ice giant, not a rocky planet. It rotates on its side, so its seasons are strange compared with Earth. Methane in the air gives it a blue-green color.

objects.name: Neptune
objects.summary: The farthest planet from the Sun, and a very windy one.
objects.description: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun. It is an ice giant, darker blue than Uranus, and it has the fastest winds measured on any planet.

groups.name: Dwarf Planets
groups.summary: Dwarf planets orbit the Sun and are round enough to be planet-like, but they have not cleared their orbits.
groups.description: Dwarf planets orbit the Sun and are round enough to be planet-like, but they have not cleared their orbits. Pluto is the famous one. Ceres is in the asteroid belt. Eris and Makemake are out past Neptune. Pick one to see its stats.

objects.name: Pluto
objects.summary: Used to be the ninth planet. Now it is the best-known dwarf planet.
objects.description: Pluto was called the ninth planet for a long time. It is now grouped as a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt. Its largest moon, Charon, is big enough that the two orbit a point between them.

objects.name: Ceres
objects.summary: The dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.
objects.description: Ceres is the only dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, between Mars and Jupiter. It is much smaller than Pluto. Bright spots on the surface are salt deposits.

objects.name: Eris
objects.summary: About Pluto's size, but much farther from the Sun.
objects.description: Eris is a dwarf planet out past Neptune. It is close to Pluto in size, but its orbit takes it much farther from the Sun. Finding Eris was a big reason Pluto got reclassified.

objects.name: Makemake
objects.summary: A Kuiper Belt dwarf planet with one known moon.
objects.description: Makemake is another Kuiper Belt dwarf planet. It is smaller than Pluto and does not have a thick atmosphere. A small moon was found around it in 2015.

groups.name: Notable Moons
groups.description: These are moons, not planets. They orbit a planet. Because of that, the distance for each moon is measured from that planet, not from the Sun. That is a different kind of number than the planets use.

objects.name: Earth's Moon
objects.summary: The moon we see at night, and the reason we have tides.
objects.description: This is Earth's moon. It has almost no air, so the surface temperature changes a lot between day and night. Its gravity is what pulls the ocean tides.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: About 120°C in daylight and -130°C at night

objects.name: Europa
objects.summary: An icy moon of Jupiter that may have an ocean under the ice.
objects.description: Europa orbits Jupiter. The outside is ice, and there is strong evidence for a saltwater ocean under that ice. That is why it shows up in so many talks about life beyond Earth.

objects.name: Titan
objects.summary: Saturn's big moon, with thick air and methane lakes.
objects.description: Titan is Saturn's largest moon. It is unusual because it has a thick atmosphere. The lakes on Titan are liquid methane and ethane, not water.

objects.name: Ganymede
objects.summary: Jupiter's largest moon, and bigger than Mercury.
objects.description: Ganymede orbits Jupiter and is the largest moon in the solar system. It is bigger than the planet Mercury. It is also the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.
